capturing, contextualizing, validating, sharing, retrieving, and applying a lesson
the difference between a local retrospective insight and reusable project learning

claims.claim: A lessons-learned process can include collecting, analyzing, saving or archiving, and sharing knowledge from positive and negative experiences.
Validation matters because it checks the accuracy of a proposed lesson and its applicability to other projects.
A lesson without context may be difficult to retrieve or adapt; the PMI case discussion identifies retrieval and adaptation as practical problems when lessons are stored in a large database.
PMI's knowledge-transfer report describes a progression of identifying relevant knowledge, capturing and retaining it, making it available, applying it, and assessing its value.
A retrospective can generate candidate observations, but a reusable lesson requires a separate decision about evidence, context, and relevance beyond that conversation.
Knowledge capture does not guarantee reuse or project outcomes; access, context, privacy, authority, and local conditions can constrain what should be recorded or applied.

correctionsNeeded: Replaced generic boilerplate with an evidence-informed explanation of capture, validation, context, retrieval, and reuse.
Added limits so an archived note is not presented as a guaranteed improvement or universally applicable rule.
Separated lessons learned from retrospective reflection and project closure.
rightsIssues: All sources are used for verification and attribution. The lesson contains original prose and no proprietary template, database design, or organization-specific procedure.

sourceRecords.title: Project Management: DOE and NNSA Should Improve Their Lessons-Learned Process for Capital Asset Projects (GAO-19-25)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live from GAO's official PDF. Supports the bounded description of a lessons-learned process (collect, analyze, save/archive, share/disseminate) and the need to validate accuracy and applicability. Agency findings are used only as a general educational example, not as requirements for other organizations.

sourceRecords.title: Capturing the Value of Project Management Through Knowledge Transfer
sourceRecords.notes: Read live from PMI's official PDF. Supports the knowledge-transfer progression of identifying, capturing/retaining, making available, applying, and assessing knowledge, and the distinction between capture and subsequent use. No report wording or framework template is reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Lessons (Really) Learned? How To Retain Project Knowledge And Avoid Recurring Nightmares
sourceRecords.notes: Read live from PMI's official site. Supports the practical caution that a large repository can be hard to search and that a candidate lesson must be understandable and retrievable in a relevant future context. It is treated as a case-oriented professional source, not as a universal prescription.
